query: Which material can be used for enhanced catalytic activity and durability toward HER and HOR, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Nanostructured high-entropy alloy (HEA) catalysts with controlled compositional tuning (via combinatorial synthesis and post-annealing) can deliver both enhanced catalytic activity and improved durability for HER and HOR compared to conventional Pt-based catalysts. This is due to the tuned d-band center and multi-element synergistic effects that optimize hydrogen adsorption/desorption energetics and provide superior corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited nanostructured HEA film comprising multiple transition metals in near-equiatomic proportions, exhibiting a random elemental distribution with potential amorphous or nanocrystalline structure.
generation.intervention: Application of controlled annealing and precise composition tuning via combinatorial synthesis to restructure the nanostructure and fine-tune the elemental surface states.
generation.conditions: Electrochemical testing conducted under realistic HER and HOR operating conditions (acidic and/or alkaline media) with cyclic voltammetry and durability cycling that mimic operational fuel cells or electrolyzers.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanostructured HEA phase featuring a tailored distribution of elements that adjusts the d-band state at the surface, promoting optimal hydrogen binding and increased resistance to corrosion.
generation.mechanism: The controlled compositional adjustment optimizes the d-band center, improving hydrogen adsorption/desorption kinetics critical for HER and HOR, while the intrinsic multi-element synergy enhances structural stability and corrosion resistance under harsh electrochemical conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tailored nanostructured HEA catalyst is expected to exhibit lower overpotentials and higher current densities for both HER and HOR, with a slower degradation rate over prolonged cycling compared to both untreated HEA films and conventional Pt-based catalysts.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of standard Pt-based catalysts and as-deposited (untreated) HEA films under identical electrochemical conditions.
generation.boundary: This outcome is predicted under controlled laboratory conditions; variations in electrolyte pH, temperature, or potential cycling protocols may affect the degree of observed performance enhancements. Scaling to practical device sizes may introduce additional challenges.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in catalytic activity and long-term durability, as well as the optimal compositional window for these HEAs, remain to be fully determined through experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: (1) nanostructured HEA films that have undergone controlled annealing and compositional tuning, and (2) control samples consisting of as-deposited HEA films and conventional Pt-based catalysts. Test all samples in identical electrochemical cells under both acidic and alkaline conditions using cyclic voltammetry and chronoamperometry. Assess performance metrics over extended cycling to evaluate degradation rates.
measurements: Overpotential required to reach a set current density for HER and HOR
Tafel slopes derived from polarization curves
Durability metrics such as percentage retention of current density after prolonged cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tailored HEA catalysts do not show a statistically significant improvement (lower overpotentials, higher current densities, and enhanced durability) compared to both the as-deposited HEA controls and the Pt-based catalysts under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. decision.trend: Over the past several years, researchers have been exploring high-entropy and refractory alloys that boast extreme stability and resistance under harsh conditions – whether that be against irradiation, high‐temperature deformation, or aggressive electrochemical/chemical environments. Early work focused on controlling microstructural evolution and phase stability through novel synthesis techniques (e.g., sputtering, laser powder bed fusion) and thermal treatments to improve durability. Later studies demonstrated that by tailoring the alloy composition and processing parameters, one can systematically enhance the robustness (e.g., resistance to dislocation formation, grain growth, and even electrochemical corrosion in NaCl solutions) while maintaining performance. Although these approaches have successfully addressed mechanical and radiation durability demands, their translation to catalytic applications (specifically for HER and HOR) remains an open frontier.
decision.unsolved: The open question is how to leverage the design insights from durable high-entropy and refractory alloys to simultaneously optimize catalytic activity and long‐term stability under the highly corrosive, cycling conditions of HER and HOR. In particular, tuning electronic properties and surface structure for enhanced catalytic function while retaining the durability benefits seen in these alloy systems remains unsolved.
decision.lever: nanostructured high-entropy alloy catalysts with tailored elemental composition (via combinatorial synthesis and controlled annealing) that tune d-band states at the surface
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of using composition-driven design to achieve enhanced durability in extreme environments as seen in previous work. By harnessing the multi-element synergy of high-entropy alloys and employing combinatorial synthesis under conditions that mimic HER and HOR operation, researchers can target both the catalytic electronic properties and the corrosion resistance required. This strategy occupies the open‐question niche, with a material intervention using the composition lever, as recommended by the previously verified niche move.
